docs.title: Why This Course Matters
docs.text:
Non-profit organizations face unprecedented challenges: growing demand for services, shrinking resources, increasing competition for funding, and rising expectations for measurable impact. Artificial Intelligence offers a transformative solution — but only when implemented thoughtfully, ethically, and in alignment with organizational mission.

Real Impact

Organizations successfully integrating AI report:

  • 3x increase in operational efficiency
  • 40% reduction in administrative time
  • 2x improvement in donor retention
  • 50% faster program delivery at scale

Source: Non-Profit Technology Network (NTEN), 2025

This course bridges the gap between AI innovation and mission-driven impact, providing practical guidance specifically tailored for organizations like Asian Media Access that serve diverse communities through education, technology, and organizing.

docs.title: Course Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

Knowledge & Understanding (Bloom's 1-2)

  • Define 200+ AI and non-profit technology concepts
  • Explain how AI algorithms work and their applications
  • Understand ethical implications and privacy requirements
  • Recognize opportunities and challenges for your organization

Application (Bloom's 3)

  • Implement AI chatbots for community engagement
  • Deploy AI-powered fundraising and donor management tools
  • Use generative AI for multilingual content creation
  • Apply automation to streamline operations

Analysis & Evaluation (Bloom's 4-5)

  • Evaluate AI vendors and tools for your needs
  • Analyze cost-benefit tradeoffs and ROI
  • Assess bias, fairness, and ethical concerns
  • Critique AI implementation strategies

Synthesis & Creation (Bloom's 6)

  • Design comprehensive AI integration strategies
  • Create governance frameworks and policies
  • Develop custom AI workflows
  • Build sustainable AI capabilities

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: AI Integration for Non-Profit Organizations is a comprehensive, pedagogically-designed textbook developed specifically for mission-driven organizations. Created in partnership with Asian Media Access, this course bridges the gap between cutting-edge AI technology and community-centered non-profit work.

docs.title: Mission-First Approach
docs.text: Every aspect of this course prioritizes organizational mission over technological capability. We believe AI should serve people and communities, not the other way around.

docs.title: Equity & Inclusion
docs.text: Special attention to serving marginalized communities, multilingual populations, and organizations with limited resources.

docs.title: Practical & Actionable
docs.text: Real tools, real budgets, real constraints. No theoretical concepts without practical application.

docs.title: Ethics at the Core
docs.text: Responsible AI isn't an add-on — it's integrated into every chapter, every example, every recommendation.

docs.title: Pedagogical Design
docs.text:
This course follows evidence-based instructional design principles:

  • Bloom's Taxonomy: Systematic cognitive development from knowledge to creation
  • Scaffolded Learning: Progressive complexity with clear prerequisites
  • Active Learning: Hands-on MicroSims and projects, not just reading
  • Mixed Media: Text, visuals, interactives, and assessments
  • Spaced Repetition: Concepts revisited and reinforced throughout

Course Overview
docs.text: This comprehensive textbook provides non-profit organizations with practical, actionable guidance for integrating artificial intelligence technologies across all operational areas. Designed specifically for organizations like Asian Media Access that serve diverse communities through multimedia education, technology, and community organizing, this course bridges the gap between AI innovation and mission-driven impact.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text:
Primary Learners: - Non-profit staff members (all levels, beginner to advanced) - Executive directors and organizational leaders - Program managers and coordinators - Technical staff and IT administrators - Volunteers and community organizers - Board members and strategic advisors

Prerequisites: - Basic computer literacy - Familiarity with non-profit operations - No prior AI or programming experience required

docs.title: Course Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this course, learners will be able to:

Knowledge Level (Remember & Understand): - Define key AI terminology and concepts relevant to non-profit operations - Identify different types of AI technologies and their applications - Recognize ethical considerations in AI deployment for mission-driven organizations - Understand data privacy requirements and community trust implications

Application Level (Apply): - Implement AI tools for fundraising, donor management, and grant writing - Deploy AI solutions for program delivery and community engagement - Apply AI technologies to streamline administrative and operational tasks - Use AI for content creation, translation, and multilingual communication

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text: Answers to 100+ common questions about AI for non-profits.

docs.title: Q: We're a small non-profit with a $200K budget. Is AI too expensive for us?
docs.text: A: No! Many AI tools offer free tiers or non-profit discounts. Start with free tools like ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, or Claude for content creation. Many CRM systems include AI features at no extra cost. Your initial investment might be just staff time for learning and setup.

docs.title: Q: Do we need technical staff to use AI?
docs.text: A: Not necessarily. Many modern AI tools are designed for non-technical users with intuitive interfaces. However, having at least one staff member who's comfortable learning new technology is helpful. Consider partnering with organizations like Asian Media Access that offer training programs.

docs.title: Q: How long does AI implementation take?
docs.text: A: It varies widely. Simple tools (like using ChatGPT for content creation) can be adopted in days. Comprehensive CRM implementation with AI features might take 3-6 months. Our recommendation: Start small with quick wins, then expand gradually.

docs.title: Q: What if our staff resist using AI?
docs.text:
A: Resistance is normal! Address it through:

  • Clear communication about how AI supports (not replaces) staff
  • Training and ongoing support
  • Celebrating early wins
  • Involving staff in selection and implementation
  • Starting with tools that make their jobs easier

docs.title: Q: How do we measure if AI is working?
docs.text:
A: Define success metrics before implementation. Examples:

  • Time saved on repetitive tasks
  • Increased donor retention rates
  • More program participants reached
  • Cost per outcome delivered
  • Staff satisfaction scores

docs.title: Q: How do we ensure AI doesn't harm the communities we serve?
docs.text:
A: Follow these principles:

  • Always prioritize community trust over efficiency
  • Be transparent about AI use
  • Test for bias regularly
  • Give people opt-out options
  • Never use AI for high-stakes decisions without human oversight
  • Develop an ethics framework

docs.title: Q: What about data privacy for our beneficiaries?
docs.text:
A: Critical considerations:

  • Only collect necessary data (data minimization)
  • Obtain informed consent
  • Use secure, reputable vendors
  • Never share PII with AI vendors unless absolutely necessary
  • Anonymize data when possible
  • Comply with GDPR, CCPA, and other regulations

docs.title: Q: Can AI write our grant proposals?
docs.text:
A: AI can assist but shouldn't write grants from scratch. Best use:

  • Draft initial content based on your notes
  • Refine and improve existing drafts
  • Generate compelling language
  • Check for clarity and grammar
  • Suggest data visualizations

You still need: Human insight, relationship context, authentic stories, and final review.

docs.title: Q: Will AI help us find major donors?
docs.text:
A: Yes! AI tools can:

  • Analyze giving patterns to identify upgrade potential
  • Screen donor lists for wealth indicators
  • Predict optimal ask amounts
  • Determine best contact timing
  • Personalize outreach at scale

But remember: Relationships still matter. AI identifies prospects; humans build relationships.

docs.title: Q: What's the difference between AI and machine learning?
docs.text:
A: Machine Learning (ML) is a subset of AI. All ML is AI, but not all AI is ML:

  • AI = Broad field of intelligent computer systems
  • ML = Specific approach where systems learn from data
  • Deep Learning = Advanced ML using neural networks

docs.title: Q: Do we need to hire a data scientist?
docs.text:
A: Probably not initially. Most modern AI tools don't require data science expertise. Consider hiring or consulting with a data scientist when you:

  • Have large datasets requiring custom analysis
  • Need to build proprietary models
  • Want to integrate multiple AI systems
  • Are scaling beyond off-the-shelf solutions

docs.title: Q: Which AI tools should we start with?
docs.text:
A: Based on your needs:

For Content Creation: - ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini (Free/paid tiers)

For Fundraising: - Bloomerang, DonorPerfect, or Little Green Light (with AI features)

For Operations: - Zapier (automation), DocuSign (document processing)

For Communications: - Canva (design), Grammarly (writing), DeepL (translation)

See our Tools Directory for comprehensive list.

docs.title: Q: How do we avoid vendor lock-in?
docs.text:
A: Smart strategies:

  • Choose tools with data export options
  • Avoid proprietary formats when possible
  • Maintain backups of your data
  • Build in-house expertise alongside vendor tools
  • Review contracts for exit clauses

docs.title: Q: How do we maintain our organization's "human touch" with AI?
docs.text:
A: AI should enhance, not replace, human connection:

  • Use AI for repetitive tasks, freeing staff for relationship-building
  • Always have human oversight for sensitive communications
  • Be transparent about what's automated vs. personal
  • Design AI interactions to feel helpful, not impersonal
  • Regularly gather feedback from your community

docs.title: Q: Can AI understand cultural nuance?
docs.text:
A: Current AI has limitations with cultural context:

  • May miss subtleties in non-Western cultures
  • Can perpetuate stereotypes from training data
  • May not understand specific community terminology

Best practices: - Always have humans from the community review AI outputs - Test AI tools with your specific community - Provide cultural context in prompts - Use AI as a draft, not final product

docs.title: Q: Will AI replace non-profit jobs?
docs.text:
A: AI will transform jobs, not eliminate them:

  • Automated: Repetitive administrative tasks
  • Enhanced: Strategic planning, relationship building
  • Emerging: AI trainers, ethics officers, automation specialists

Focus on developing skills AI can't replicate: empathy, creative problem-solving, community relationship building.

A: Key trends for non-profits:

  • More affordable, accessible tools
  • Better multilingual capabilities
  • Improved bias detection and fairness
  • Stronger privacy protections
  • Industry-specific AI solutions for non-profits

docs.title: Accuracy
docs.text:
The proportion of correct predictions made by an AI model.

Example: A donor retention model with 85% accuracy correctly predicts whether 85 out of 100 donors will give again.

docs.title: AI Agent
docs.text:
An autonomous AI system that can plan and execute complex tasks.

Example: An AI agent that monitors your social media, identifies engagement opportunities, drafts responses, and schedules posts.

docs.title: Algorithmic Bias
docs.text:
Systematic errors in AI systems that create unfair outcomes for certain groups.

Example: A grant recommendation system trained primarily on data from large urban non-profits might unfairly score rural organizations lower.

docs.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
docs.text:
Computer systems capable of performing tasks requiring human intelligence.

Example: A chatbot that answers donor questions 24/7 without human intervention.

docs.title: Chatbot
docs.text:
AI-powered conversational assistant providing automated responses.

Example: A chatbot on your website answering FAQs about volunteer opportunities, donation methods, and program schedules.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
Task of categorizing data into predefined classes.

Example: Automatically categorizing support emails as "donations," "volunteer inquiries," or "program questions."

docs.title: CRM (Constituent Relationship Management)
docs.text:
Database managing relationships with supporters.

Example: Salesforce Nonprofit Cloud tracking donor history, volunteer hours, and event attendance.

docs.title: Data Privacy
docs.text:
Protection of personal information from unauthorized access.

Example: Encrypting beneficiary data and limiting staff access based on role.

docs.title: Deep Learning
docs.text:
Machine learning using neural networks with multiple layers.

Example: Image recognition identifying people in event photos for automatic tagging.

docs.title: Generative AI
docs.text:
AI systems creating new content (text, images, audio, video).

Example: Using ChatGPT to draft newsletter content or DALL-E to create event graphics.

docs.title: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation)
docs.text:
European data protection regulation.

Example: Ensuring EU donors can request deletion of their data from your system.

docs.title: Large Language Model (LLM)
docs.text:
AI model trained on vast text data to understand and generate language.

Example: GPT-4, Claude, or Gemini powering your grant writing assistance tool.

docs.title: Machine Learning (ML)
docs.text:
Systems learning from data without explicit programming.

Example: Analyzing past donation patterns to predict which current donors are likely to increase their giving.

docs.title: Natural Language Processing (NLP)
docs.text:
AI's ability to understand and generate human language.

Example: Automatically translating your website content into Spanish, Hmong, and Vietnamese.

docs.title: Neural Network
docs.text:
Computing system inspired by biological neural networks.

Example: The underlying architecture enabling facial recognition or voice transcription.

docs.title: Predictive Analytics
docs.text:
Using data to forecast future outcomes.

Example: Predicting which volunteers are at risk of disengaging so you can intervene early.

docs.title: Prompt
docs.text:
Input text given to an AI model to generate a response.

Example: "Write a 200-word thank-you email for a first-time $100 donor to our youth program."

docs.title: Prompt Engineering
docs.text:
Crafting effective prompts to get desired AI outputs.

Example: Adding "Be warm but professional, mention specific program impact" to improve output quality.

docs.title: ROI (Return on Investment)
docs.text:
Measuring financial value of AI initiatives.

Example: Calculating that your $5,000 AI chatbot investment saved 200 staff hours worth $10,000.

docs.title: Sentiment Analysis
docs.text:
Determining emotional tone in feedback or communications.

Example: Analyzing program evaluation surveys to identify patterns in participant satisfaction.

docs.title: Token
docs.text:
Basic unit of text processed by language models.

Example: The sentence "AI helps non-profits" contains roughly 5 tokens.

docs.title: Training Data
docs.text:
Dataset used to teach an AI model.

Example: Using 5 years of donation records to train a model predicting donor retention.

docs.text: Welcome to your journey into AI integration for mission-driven organizations!

docs.title: 1.1 What is Artificial Intelligence?
docs.text:
Imagine a computer system that can understand your questions, write compelling grant proposals, translate your newsletters into multiple languages, and predict which donors are most likely to give—all while you focus on serving your community.

This isn't science fiction. This is artificial intelligence (AI), and it's transforming how non-profit organizations operate.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the capability of computer systems to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence. These tasks include understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions, and solving problems.

Think of AI as a highly capable assistant that can:

  • ✅ Process information faster than any human
  • ✅ Find patterns in massive amounts of data
  • ✅ Work 24/7 without getting tired
  • ✅ Handle repetitive tasks consistently
  • ✅ Learn and improve over time

docs.title: Real-World Example: Asian Media Access
docs.text:
At Asian Media Access, AI could help automatically translate educational materials into Hmong, Vietnamese, Karen, and other languages spoken by the communities they serve—ensuring no one is left behind due to language barriers.

Key Concept

AI isn't about replacing humans; it's about augmenting human capabilities so non-profit staff can focus on mission-critical work that requires empathy, creativity, and community connection.

docs.title: 1.2 The AI Revolution and Non-Profit Sector
docs.text:
The non-profit sector has historically been cautious about adopting new technologies. Budget constraints, limited technical staff, and a focus on direct service delivery often mean that technological innovation takes a back seat.

However, AI presents a unique opportunity that non-profits cannot afford to ignore.

docs.title: Why Now?
docs.text:
1. Accessibility - AI tools are more affordable and user-friendly than ever
  2. Cloud-Based Solutions - No need for expensive infrastructure
  3. Competition for Funding - Donors increasingly expect data-driven impact
  4. Efficiency Imperative - Doing more with less resources
  5. Scale Potential - Reach more beneficiaries without proportional cost increases

Case Study: DonorsChoose

DonorsChoose.org used AI to analyze teacher requests and match them with donors based on interests and giving history.

Result: 30% increase in funding success rate and $15M additional funds distributed to classrooms.

docs.title: 1.3 Why AI Matters for Asian Media Access
docs.text: Asian Media Access's mission is to connect the disconnected through multimedia arts, technology, and community organizing. AI directly supports this mission in multiple ways:

docs.title: Multilingual Communication at Scale
docs.text: AI translation tools can instantly convert educational content, event information, and program descriptions into the many languages of the AAPI community—ensuring accessibility for immigrants and refugees.

docs.title: Program Impact Measurement
docs.text: AI can analyze program participation data, participant feedback, and community outcomes to demonstrate impact to funders and guide program improvements.

docs.title: Volunteer Coordination
docs.text: With AI-powered scheduling and matching tools, AMA can optimize volunteer placement in their e-Magine training programs and multimedia education initiatives.

docs.title: Fundraising Enhancement
docs.text: AI can identify potential major donors, personalize outreach, and optimize fundraising campaigns—critical for sustainability.

docs.title: Content Creation
docs.text: AI assists in creating social media posts, grant proposals, and educational materials—extending staff capacity without additional hiring.

docs.title: 1.4 Common Misconceptions About AI
docs.text:
Let's bust some myths:

Myth Reality "AI is too expensive" Many tools have free tiers or non-profit discounts "AI will replace staff" AI augments work, freeing staff for high-value tasks "AI is only for tech companies" Non-profits are successfully using AI across sectors "We need data scientists" Modern AI tools are designed for non-technical users "AI is unethical" Ethical AI is possible with the right approach

docs.title: 1.5 The AI Opportunity
docs.text: AI offers three major benefits for non-profits:

docs.title: 1. Efficiency Gains
docs.text:
Automate repetitive tasks like data entry, email responses, and report generation. Free staff time for strategic work.

Example: Automated donor thank-you emails save 10 hours/week.

docs.title: 2. Enhanced Impact
docs.text:
Personalize services, predict needs, and reach more people with the same resources.

Example: AI chatbot answers 80% of volunteer questions 24/7.

docs.title: 3. Better Decision-Making
docs.text:
Analyze data to understand what works, predict outcomes, and optimize programs.

Example: Predict which donors are likely to lapse and intervene proactively.

docs.title: 1.6 Ethical Considerations Preview
docs.text:
We'll dive deep into ethics in Chapter 4, but here are core principles:

Ethics First

  1. Community Trust - Prioritize trust over efficiency
  2. Transparency - Be open about AI use
  3. Fairness - Test for and eliminate bias
  4. Privacy - Protect personal information
  5. Human Oversight - Never fully automate high-stakes decisions

docs.title: Chapter 2: AI Fundamentals - Core Concepts
docs.text: Understanding how AI actually works under the hood.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Explain the difference between AI, machine learning, and deep learning
  • Understand supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning

docs.title: 2.1 Machine Learning Explained
docs.text: Machine Learning (ML) is a subset of AI where systems learn from data without being explicitly programmed for every scenario.

docs.title: The Traditional Programming vs. Machine Learning
docs.text:
Traditional Programming: 

Rules + Data → Answers
You write explicit rules, give it data, and get answers.

Machine Learning: 

Data + Answers → Rules
You give examples (data + correct answers), and the system learns the rules.

docs.title: Example: Email Spam Filter
docs.text:
Traditional: Write rules like "if email contains 'FREE MONEY', mark as spam" - Problem: Spammers adapt, endless rule updates needed

Machine Learning: Show the system 10,000 spam emails and 10,000 legitimate emails - System learns patterns automatically - Adapts to new spam tactics

Non-Profit Application

Use ML to predict which donors are likely to give again, which volunteers might drop out, or which programs will have the most impact.

docs.title: Supervised Learning
docs.text:
Definition: Learning from labeled examples (data with correct answers).

How it works: 1. Provide training data with labels (input → correct output) 2. Model learns patterns 3. Model predicts labels for new, unseen data

Examples: - Email classification: Spam or not spam - Donor prediction: Will give or won't give - Image recognition: This is a cat, this is a dog

Non-Profit Use Cases: - Predict donor retention - Classify grant applications - Identify at-risk program participants

docs.title: Unsupervised Learning
docs.text:
Definition: Finding patterns in data without labels.

How it works: 1. Provide unlabeled data 2. Model finds hidden patterns and groups 3. Discovers structure you didn't know existed

Examples: - Customer segmentation: Group similar donors together - Anomaly detection: Find unusual spending patterns - Topic modeling: Discover themes in survey responses

Non-Profit Use Cases: - Segment donors for targeted campaigns - Identify volunteer clusters (weekend warriors, skill specialists, etc.) - Find patterns in program feedback

docs.title: Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
Definition: Learning through trial and error with rewards.

How it works: 1. Agent takes actions in an environment 2. Receives rewards (positive) or penalties (negative) 3. Learns to maximize rewards over time

Examples: - Game playing (Chess, Go) - Robotics - Resource allocation optimization

Non-Profit Use Cases: - Optimize email send times - Resource allocation across programs - Dynamic pricing for fundraising events

docs.title: What is a Neural Network?
docs.text:
A neural network is a computing system inspired by biological brains. It consists of:

  • Input layer: Receives data
  • Hidden layers: Process information
  • Output layer: Produces results

docs.title: Simple Analogy
docs.text:
Think of a neural network like a series of filters:

Raw data → Filter 1 → Filter 2 → Filter 3 → Decision

Each filter extracts increasingly complex features.

Example - Photo recognition: - Layer 1: Detects edges - Layer 2: Detects shapes - Layer 3: Detects objects - Output: "This is a person"

docs.title: Deep Learning
docs.text:
Definition: Neural networks with many hidden layers (hence "deep").

Why it matters: Deep networks can learn very complex patterns that traditional ML can't.

Applications: - Language translation - Image generation - Voice recognition - Self-driving cars

Non-Profit Applications: - Multilingual content translation - Image classification for visual archives - Voice-to-text for accessibility

docs.title: 2.4 Natural Language Processing (NLP)
docs.text: NLP is AI's ability to understand and generate human language.

docs.title: Key NLP Tasks
docs.text: Task Description Non-Profit Example Text Classification Categorize text Sort donor emails by intent Sentiment Analysis Detect emotion Analyze program feedback Translation Convert languages Translate materials for AAPI communities Named Entity Recognition Identify names, places Extract donor info from emails Text Generation Create new text Draft thank-you letters Question Answering Answer queries Chatbot for volunteer questions

docs.title: How NLP Works
docs.text:
1. Tokenization: Break text into words/pieces
  2. Embedding: Convert words to numbers
  3. Processing: Neural network analyzes patterns
  4. Output: Classification, generation, or translation

docs.title: 2.5 Computer Vision
docs.text: Computer vision is AI's ability to interpret and understand visual information.

docs.title: Key Vision Tasks
docs.text: Task Description Non-Profit Example Image Classification What's in this image? Categorize event photos Object Detection Where are objects? Count people at events Face Recognition Who is this? Event check-in systems OCR Extract text from images Digitize paper records Image Generation Create images Generate social media graphics

docs.text:

docs.title: 2.6 How AI Models Learn from Data
The Training Process
docs.text:
1. Collect Data: Gather examples (more is better)
  2. Prepare Data: Clean, organize, label
  3. Split Data:
  4. Training set (80%): Teach the model
  5. Validation set (10%): Tune the model
  6. Test set (10%): Final evaluation
  7. Train Model: Feed training data, adjust parameters
  8. Evaluate: Test on unseen data
  9. Deploy: Use in real world
  10. Monitor: Track performance, retrain as needed

docs.title: Example: Donor Retention Model
docs.text:
1. Collect: 5 years of donor data
2. Prepare: Clean addresses, categorize giving levels
3. Split: 80% train, 10% validate, 10% test
4. Train: Model learns patterns of repeat donors
5. Evaluate: 85% accuracy on test set
6. Deploy: Score current donors for retention risk
7. Monitor: Retrain quarterly with new data

docs.title: Model Performance Metrics
docs.text:
Accuracy: Percentage of correct predictions 

Accuracy = Correct Predictions / Total Predictions

Precision: Of items marked positive, how many are actually positive? 

Precision = True Positives / (True Positives + False Positives)

Recall: Of actual positive items, how many did we find? 

Recall = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives)

F1 Score: Balance of precision and recall 

F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

docs.title: When to Use Each Metric
docs.text:
• Accuracy: Balanced datasets, general performance
  • Precision: When false positives are costly (spam detection)
  • Recall: When false negatives are costly (disease detection)
  • F1: When you need balance between precision and recall

docs.title: Overfitting
docs.text:
Problem: Model memorizes training data instead of learning patterns.

Signs: - Perfect training performance - Poor performance on new data

Solutions: - Use more training data - Simplify the model - Use regularization techniques

docs.title: Underfitting
docs.text:
Problem: Model is too simple to capture patterns.

Signs: - Poor training performance - Poor test performance

Solutions: - Use more complex model - Add more features - Train longer

docs.title: Data Quality Issues
docs.text:
Problem: Garbage in, garbage out.

Common Issues: - Missing data - Incorrect labels - Biased sampling - Outdated information

Solutions: - Clean data thoroughly - Validate labels - Ensure representative sampling - Update regularly

docs.text:

docs.title: 3.1 What is Generative AI?
docs.text: Generative AI creates new content—text, images, audio, video—based on patterns learned from training data.

docs.title: Traditional AI vs. Generative AI
docs.text: Traditional AI Generative AI Classifies existing data Creates new content "Is this spam?" "Write an email" "What's in this image?" "Generate an image" Analyzes patterns Produces original outputs

docs.title: Real-World Applications
docs.text:
• Text: Write emails, articles, reports, social media posts
  • Images: Create graphics, illustrations, photos
  • Code: Generate software programs
  • Audio: Compose music, generate voices
  • Video: Create animations, edit videos

docs.title: 3.2 Large Language Models (LLMs)
docs.text: LLMs are AI models trained on vast amounts of text to understand and generate human language.

docs.title: Popular LLMs
docs.text:
• ChatGPT (OpenAI) - General purpose, widely used
  • Claude (Anthropic) - Focused on safety, helpful for analysis
  • Gemini (Google) - Integrated with Google services
  • Llama (Meta) - Open source option

docs.title: How LLMs Work
docs.text:
1. Training: Learn patterns from billions of web pages, books, articles
  2. Tokenization: Break text into small pieces (tokens)
  3. Prediction: Predict next most likely token based on context
  4. Generation: String predictions together to form coherent text

docs.title: LLM Capabilities
docs.text: ✅ Writing and editing ✅ Translation ✅ Summarization ✅ Question answering ✅ Code generation ✅ Data analysis ✅ Creative brainstorming ✅ Formatting and organizing

docs.title: 3.3 The Art of Prompting
docs.text: A prompt is your instruction to an AI model. Good prompts get good results.

docs.title: Basic Prompt Structure
docs.text:
[Context] + [Task] + [Format] + [Constraints]

Example: 

Context: You are a fundraising expert for non-profits.
Task: Write a donor thank-you email.
Format: Keep it under 200 words, warm and personal.
Constraints: Mention the $500 gift supported youth programs.

docs.title: Prompt Engineering Tips
docs.text:
Effective Prompts

  1. Be Specific - "Write a 100-word email" not "write an email"
  2. Give Context - Explain who you are, what you need
  3. Provide Examples - Show the style/format you want
  4. Iterate - Refine based on outputs
  5. Use Roles - "Act as a grant writing expert..."

docs.title: Common Prompt Patterns
docs.text:
Few-Shot Learning: 

Example 1: [input] → [output]
Example 2: [input] → [output]
Now do: [your input]

Chain of Thought: 

Let's think step-by-step:
1. First, analyze...
2. Then, consider...
3. Finally, conclude...

Template Filling: 

Fill in this template:
Subject: [catchy subject line]
Body: [personalized greeting]
...

docs.title: Content Creation
docs.text:
Use Case: Draft social media posts

Prompt: 

Create 5 Facebook posts promoting our youth coding workshop.
Audience: Parents in AAPI communities.
Tone: Encouraging, culturally aware.
Include: Date (March 15), Free registration, Skills learned.

docs.title: Email Communications
docs.text:
Use Case: Donor thank-you emails

Prompt: 

Write a warm thank-you email to a first-time donor who gave $50.
Mention: Their gift helps provide art supplies to 10 children.
Tone: Grateful but not overly formal.
Length: 150 words.
Include: Invitation to visit our center.

docs.title: Grant Writing
docs.text:
Use Case: Draft program descriptions

Prompt: 

Write a 250-word program description for a grant proposal.
Program: Multimedia education for refugee youth
Key points: Builds tech skills, cultural expression, career pathways
Include: Outcomes, who we serve, why it matters

docs.title: Translation
docs.text:
Use Case: Multilingual outreach

Prompt: 

Translate this volunteer recruitment flyer into:
1. Spanish
2. Vietnamese  
3. Hmong

Maintain the warm, welcoming tone.
Adapt idioms if direct translation doesn't work.

docs.title: What are Tokens?
docs.text: Tokens are chunks of text that LLMs process. Roughly: - 1 token ≈ 0.75 words (English) - "Hello world" = 2 tokens - "Artificial intelligence" = 2 tokens

docs.title: Context Window
docs.text:
The context window is how much text an LLM can "remember" at once.

Model Context Window GPT-3.5 ~4,000 tokens (~3,000 words) GPT-4 ~8,000-32,000 tokens Claude ~100,000 tokens (~75,000 words) Gemini ~1 million tokens

Why it matters: - Larger context = Can process longer documents - Can "remember" entire conversations - Better for analyzing complex materials

docs.title: Temperature
docs.text:
Controls randomness in outputs:

  • 0.0 - Deterministic, predictable (good for factual tasks)
  • 0.7 - Balanced creativity and consistency
  • 1.0+ - Very creative, less predictable (good for brainstorming)

Example: 

Temperature 0.0: "Thank you for your generous donation."
Temperature 1.0: "Your incredible generosity fills our hearts with gratitude!"

docs.title: Other Parameters
docs.text:
• Max Tokens: Limit response length
  • Top-P: Alternative to temperature
  • Frequency Penalty: Avoid repetition
  • Presence Penalty: Encourage new topics

docs.title: What LLMs Can't Do (Well)
docs.text: ❌ Real-time information (unless connected to search) ❌ Complex math (without tools) ❌ Accessing private/proprietary data ❌ Perfect accuracy on all facts ❌ Understanding visual content (unless multimodal)

docs.title: Hallucinations
docs.text:
Definition: When an LLM confidently generates false information.

Why it happens: - LLMs predict plausible text, not truth - No fact-checking mechanism - Trained on internet data (including misinformation)

How to minimize: 1. Ask for sources/citations 2. Verify critical information 3. Use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) 4. Be specific: "Only use information from [source]" 5. Cross-check with multiple queries

Critical Rule

Never use LLM outputs for high-stakes decisions without human verification!

docs.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
docs.text:
Combine LLM with your own data:

  1. Store your documents in a database
  2. When user asks a question, retrieve relevant docs
  3. Feed docs + question to LLM
  4. LLM answers based on YOUR data

Non-Profit Use: Answer questions about your specific programs using only your documentation.

docs.title: Fine-Tuning
docs.text:
Train an LLM on your specific data to specialize it.

When to consider: - You have lots of domain-specific data - Generic LLMs don't capture your organization's voice - Need consistent brand messaging

Cost: Usually expensive; start with good prompting first.

docs.title: Function Calling
docs.text:
Let LLMs trigger specific actions:

User: "Email our top 10 donors about the gala"
→ LLM extracts: action=send_email, recipients=top_10_donors, content=gala_invite
→ Your system executes the action

docs.title: Bias in LLMs
docs.text:
LLMs reflect biases in training data: - Cultural stereotypes - Gender bias - Racial bias - Socioeconomic assumptions

Mitigation: - Review outputs for bias - Test with diverse perspectives - Have humans review before publishing - Provide diverse examples in prompts

docs.title: Privacy Concerns
docs.text:
Never Input

  • Personal identifiable information (PII)
  • Private donor data
  • Confidential organizational information
  • Sensitive beneficiary information

Most LLM providers use inputs for training (unless you have specific agreements).

docs.title: Copyright and Attribution
docs.text:
• LLM outputs may resemble copyrighted material
  • Always review and edit generated content
  • Add your own insights and analysis
  • Cite sources when appropriate

docs.title: Chapter 4: Ethics, Bias, and Responsible AI
docs.text: Building trust through ethical AI implementation.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand ethical principles for AI in mission-driven organizations
  • Identify different types of bias in AI systems
  • Evaluate AI implementations for fairness and equity
  • Apply responsible AI practices to your organization
  • Create ethical guidelines for AI use

Bloom's Level: 4-5 (Analyze, Evaluate) | Time: 4-5 hours

docs.title: 4.1 Why Ethics Matter More for Non-Profits
docs.text:
Non-profits operate on trust. Your community trusts you to: - Serve their best interests - Protect their privacy - Treat everyone fairly - Be transparent about your methods

AI can erode that trust quickly if implemented carelessly.

docs.title: The Stakes
docs.text:
For-Profit AI Failure Non-Profit AI Failure Bad PR, potential lawsuits Loss of community trust Stock price drops Donors leave Fix and move on Beneficiaries harmed Financial impact Mission impact

Remember

One biased AI decision can undo years of community trust-building.

docs.title: 1. Beneficence (Do Good)
docs.text:
AI should actively benefit your community and further your mission.

Questions to ask: - Does this AI genuinely help our beneficiaries? - Are we using AI because it's trendy or because it serves our mission? - Could these resources be better spent elsewhere?

docs.title: 2. Non-Maleficence (Do No Harm)
docs.text:
AI should not harm individuals or communities, even unintentionally.

Questions to ask: - Could this AI disadvantage any group? - What happens if the AI makes a mistake? - Are there unintended consequences?

docs.title: 3. Justice (Fairness)
docs.text:
AI benefits and burdens should be distributed fairly.

Questions to ask: - Who benefits from this AI? - Who bears the costs or risks? - Are we addressing existing inequities or perpetuating them?

docs.title: 4. Autonomy (Respect)
docs.text:
People should maintain control and decision-making power.

Questions to ask: - Can people opt out of AI systems? - Do they understand how AI affects them? - Have we obtained informed consent?

docs.title: 5. Transparency
docs.text:
Be open about AI use and decision-making processes.

Questions to ask: - Do stakeholders know when AI is used? - Can we explain AI decisions? - Are our criteria and methods clear?

docs.title: 4.3 Understanding Algorithmic Bias
docs.text: Bias: Systematic errors that create unfair outcomes for certain groups.

docs.title: Types of Bias
docs.text:
1. Historical Bias - Training data reflects past discrimination - Example: AI trained on historical hiring data perpetuates gender bias

2. Representation Bias - Some groups over/underrepresented in data - Example: Facial recognition trained mostly on white faces fails on darker skin tones

3. Measurement Bias - How we measure success introduces bias - Example: Defining "successful" donor based on giving amount ignores community impact

4. Aggregation Bias - One model applied to diverse groups - Example: Health AI trained on general population performs poorly for specific ethnic groups

5. Evaluation Bias - Testing doesn't include all affected groups - Example: Chatbot tested only in English misses issues with other languages

6. Deployment Bias - System used differently than intended - Example: Donor scoring tool used to exclude low-income communities

docs.title: Case 1: Recidivism Prediction
docs.text: System: COMPAS predicted likelihood of re-offending Bias: Higher false positive rates for Black defendants Impact: Unjust sentencing decisions Lesson: Historical bias in criminal justice data perpetuated discrimination

docs.title: Case 2: Facial Recognition
docs.text: System: Commercial facial recognition software Bias: 34% error rate for dark-skinned women vs. 0.8% for light-skinned men Impact: Misidentification, false accusations Lesson: Representation bias in training data

docs.title: Case 3: Job Screening AI
docs.text: System: Amazon's resume screening tool Bias: Penalized resumes with "women's" (e.g., "women's chess club") Impact: Discriminated against female candidates Lesson: Historical bias from male-dominated tech hiring

docs.title: How This Applies to Non-Profits
docs.text:
Non-Profit Scenarios

  • Grant recommendation AI favors organizations in wealthy zip codes
  • Volunteer matching system steers women toward "nurturing" roles
  • Donor prediction model undervalues community members without formal jobs
  • Service eligibility AI discriminates against immigrants without traditional documentation

docs.title: 4.5 Detecting Bias in Your AI Systems
Quantitative Methods
docs.text:
Disparate Impact Analysis 

Acceptance Rate for Group A / Acceptance Rate for Group B

If ratio < 0.80, potential disparate impact exists

Confusion Matrix by Group - Compare false positive/negative rates across demographics - Look for systematic differences

Fairness Metrics - Demographic parity - Equal opportunity - Predictive parity - Individual fairness

docs.title: Qualitative Methods
docs.text:
• Community feedback: Ask affected groups
  • Scenario testing: Try edge cases and diverse examples
  • Expert review: Have domain experts examine outputs
  • Stakeholder audits: Regular review with community members

docs.title: Pre-Processing (Fix the Data)
docs.text:
1. Collect diverse data - Ensure all groups represented
  2. Balance datasets - Oversample underrepresented groups
  3. Remove proxies - Eliminate correlated features (zip code → race)
  4. Audit for bias - Statistical testing before training

docs.title: In-Processing (Fix the Algorithm)
docs.text:
1. Fairness constraints - Build fairness into model training
  2. Adversarial debiasing - Train model to ignore sensitive attributes
  3. Regularization - Penalize biased predictions

docs.title: Post-Processing (Fix the Outputs)
docs.text:
1. Threshold adjustment - Set different decision thresholds by group
  2. Calibration - Ensure predictions equally accurate across groups
  3. Human override - Allow human review of edge cases

docs.title: Organizational Measures
docs.text:
1. Diverse teams - Include affected communities in development
  2. Regular audits - Ongoing bias testing
  3. Transparent documentation - Clear about methods and limitations
  4. Accountability - Clear responsibility for AI decisions

docs.title: 4.7 The Digital Divide
docs.text: Technology access is unequal. AI can worsen this divide.

docs.title: Dimensions of Digital Divide
docs.text:
• Access: Not everyone has internet, devices
  • Skills: Digital literacy varies widely
  • Language: Most AI optimized for English
  • Disability: Many AI tools lack accessibility features

docs.title: Ensuring Equity
docs.text: ✅ Provide multiple access paths - Phone, web, in-person ✅ Offer human alternatives - Never force AI-only interactions ✅ Support multiple languages - Especially for your communities ✅ Design for accessibility - Screen readers, captions, simple language ✅ Provide training - Help people use new tools ✅ Consider low-bandwidth - Not everyone has high-speed internet

docs.title: 4.8 Informed Consent
docs.text: People should understand and agree to AI use.

docs.title: What to Communicate
docs.text:
1. That AI is being used - "We use AI to..."
  2. How it works - Simple explanation
  3. What data is collected - Be specific
  4. How decisions are made - Key factors
  5. Rights and options - Opt-out, appeal, human review
  6. Contact information - Who to ask for help

docs.title: Example Consent Language
docs.text:
We use artificial intelligence to help match volunteers 
with opportunities. The system considers your stated interests, 
availability, and skills. You can opt out at any time and 
request human matching instead. Your information is never 
shared with third parties. Questions? Contact volunteers@org.org

docs.title: Step 1: Define Your Values
docs.text: What matters most to your organization? - Community trust - Equity and inclusion - Transparency - Beneficiary wellbeing - Data privacy

docs.title: Step 2: Establish Principles
docs.text: Translate values into actionable principles: - "We will never use AI for decisions affecting eligibility without human review" - "We will test all AI systems for bias against protected groups" - "We will provide clear opt-out options for all AI systems"

docs.title: Step 3: Create Decision Criteria
docs.text: Question Must Answer YES Does this AI advance our mission? ✓ Have we tested for bias? ✓ Can we explain decisions to stakeholders? ✓ Do affected people consent? ✓ Is there meaningful human oversight? ✓

docs.title: Step 4: Assign Responsibility
docs.text:
• Who reviews AI systems for ethics?
  • Who investigates bias complaints?
  • Who approves new AI implementations?
  • Who communicates with affected communities?

docs.title: Step 5: Regular Review
docs.text:
• Quarterly ethics audits
  • Annual community feedback sessions
  • Ongoing bias testing
  • Policy updates as needed

docs.title: DO:
docs.text: ✅ Start with low-stakes applications ✅ Be transparent about AI use ✅ Test extensively before deploying ✅ Provide human alternatives ✅ Monitor for unintended consequences ✅ Involve affected communities in decisions ✅ Document everything ✅ Update systems regularly

docs.title: DON'T:
docs.text: ❌ Use AI for high-stakes decisions without human review ❌ Assume AI is neutral or objective ❌ Deploy without bias testing ❌ Hide AI use from stakeholders ❌ Ignore complaints about bias ❌ Use AI because everyone else is ❌ Forget about people without technology access ❌ Prioritize efficiency over equity

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• Ethics are foundational, not optional, for non-profit AI
  • Multiple types of bias can creep into AI systems
  • Bias comes from data, algorithms, and deployment
  • Detect bias through quantitative and qualitative methods
  • Mitigation requires technical and organizational approaches
  • Address the digital divide proactively
  • Obtain informed consent from affected individuals
  • Build comprehensive ethics frameworks
  • Prioritize trust over convenience

docs.title: Chapter 5: Data Privacy and Security
docs.text:
Protecting personal information while leveraging AI.

Learning Objectives: Understand privacy regulations, implement data protection, ensure compliance

Time: 3-4 hours

docs.title: 5.1 Why Privacy Matters for Non-Profits
docs.text:
Your community members trust you with sensitive information. One privacy breach can: - Destroy years of trust - Lead to legal consequences - Harm vulnerable populations - End your organization

Key Regulations: - GDPR (European Union) - CCPA (California) - HIPAA (Health data) - FERPA (Education data)

docs.title: 5.2 Personal Identifiable Information (PII)
docs.text:
Direct PII: Name, SSN, email, phone, address Indirect PII: Demographics that could identify someone when combined

Protected Classes: - Health information - Financial data - Immigration status - Children's data (COPPA)

docs.title: 5.3 Data Minimization
docs.text:
Principle: Collect only what you actually need.

Questions to ask: - Do we really need this data? - How long must we keep it? - Who needs access? - What's the risk if it's exposed?

docs.title: 5.4 AI-Specific Privacy Concerns
docs.text:
1. Training Data: Personal info in AI training sets
  2. Inference Attacks: AI reveals training data
  3. Model Inversion: Reconstruct individual records
  4. Membership Inference: Determine if someone's data was used
  5. Third-Party Risk: Cloud AI services handling your data

docs.title: 5.5 Best Practices
docs.text: ✅ Anonymization - Remove identifiers ✅ Encryption - Protect data at rest and in transit ✅ Access Controls - Limit who sees what ✅ Consent Management - Clear opt-in/opt-out ✅ Regular Audits - Check compliance ✅ Incident Response Plan - Prepare for breaches ✅ Privacy by Design - Build in from start

docs.title: Chapter 11: Selecting and Evaluating AI Tools
docs.text:
Making smart technology decisions.

Learning Objectives: Assess needs, evaluate vendors, make informed decisions

docs.title: Start with Problems, Not Solutions
docs.text: Wrong approach: "Everyone's using AI chatbots, we should too" Right approach: "We spend 20 hours/week answering the same questions. How can we solve this?"

docs.title: Assessment Framework
docs.text:
1. Identify Pain Points - What takes too much time? - Where do errors occur? - What limits our scale? - What frustrates staff? - Where do we lose people?

2. Quantify Impact - Hours spent per week - Cost of current approach - Opportunity cost - Error rates - Staff satisfaction scores

3. Define Success - Specific metrics - Target improvements - Timeline - Budget

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria
docs.text: Criterion Questions Weight Functionality Does it solve our problem? 30% Usability Can staff use it easily? 20% Integration Works with existing tools? 15% Cost Within budget? Hidden fees? 15% Support Help when needed? 10% Security Meets privacy standards? 10%

docs.title: The Scorecard Method
docs.text: Rate each vendor 1-5 on each criterion, multiply by weight, sum total.

docs.title: Testing Before Buying
docs.text: Steps: 1. Start with free trial (most offer 14-30 days) 2. Define specific test scenarios 3. Involve actual users 4. Measure results 5. Document pros/cons 6. Compare to alternatives

docs.title: What to Test
docs.text: ✅ Core functionality ✅ Integration with existing tools ✅ Staff learning curve ✅ Support responsiveness ✅ Performance under load ✅ Data export (can you leave?)

docs.title: Beyond Subscription Fees
docs.text:
Direct Costs: - Monthly/annual subscription - Per-user fees - Implementation fees - Training costs - Integration costs

Indirect Costs: - Staff time to manage - Learning curve productivity loss - Ongoing maintenance - Potential switching costs

docs.title: ROI Calculation
docs.text:
ROI = (Benefits - Costs) / Costs × 100%

Example:
Benefits: $20,000/year (time saved)
Costs: $5,000/year (subscription + time)
ROI = ($20,000 - $5,000) / $5,000 = 300%

docs.text: ❌ Shiny Object Syndrome - Buying because it's trendy ❌ Over-Engineering - Too complex for needs ❌ Under-Researching - First option seems good enough ❌ Ignoring Integration - Creates data silos ❌ Skipping Training - Staff won't adopt ❌ No Success Metrics - Can't tell if it's working

docs.title: Chapter 12: Measuring AI Impact and ROI
docs.text:
Demonstrating value and optimizing performance.

Learning Objectives: Define metrics, calculate ROI, communicate impact

Time: 3-4 hours

docs.title: 12.1 Why Measurement Matters
docs.text: For funders: Demonstrate responsible stewardship For board: Justify technology investments For staff: Show their time is valued For beneficiaries: Prove we're effective

docs.title: Efficiency Metrics
docs.text:
Time Savings: - Hours saved per week - Tasks automated - Faster processes

Cost Reduction: - Labor cost savings - Error reduction costs - Resource optimization

docs.title: Effectiveness Metrics
docs.text:
Quality: - Accuracy improvements - Error rate reduction - Consistency gains

Scale: - More people served - Broader reach - Faster response

docs.title: Impact Metrics
docs.text:
Mission Outcomes: - Program completion rates - Beneficiary satisfaction - Long-term success rates

Organizational Health: - Staff satisfaction - Retention improvement - Capacity growth

docs.title: Simple ROI Formula
docs.text: ROI = (Gains - Investment) / Investment × 100%

docs.title: Comprehensive Example
docs.text:
Investment: - AI tool subscription: $6,000/year - Implementation time: $2,000 - Training: $1,000 - Total: $9,000

Gains: - Time saved: 15 hrs/week × $25/hr × 52 weeks = $19,500 - Error reduction: $2,000/year - Increased revenue: $3,000/year - Total: $24,500

ROI: ($24,500 - $9,000) / $9,000 = 172%

docs.text:

docs.title: Chapter 13: Organizational AI Strategy and Roadmap
docs.text:
Building a sustainable AI future.

Learning Objectives: Develop strategy, create roadmaps, plan for sustainability

Time: 4-5 hours

docs.title: Vision Statement Elements
docs.text:
Components: 1. Where you are now (current state) 2. Where you want to be (future state) 3. Why AI matters to your mission 4. How AI aligns with values 5. Timeline (3-5 years)

Example: 

"By 2028, [Organization] will leverage AI to serve 50% more 
families while maintaining personalized, culturally responsive 
care. AI will handle routine tasks, freeing staff to focus on 
relationship-building and complex case management. We will be 
recognized as a leader in ethical, equitable AI use in the 
non-profit sector."

docs.title: Prioritization Framework
docs.text:
Impact vs. Effort Matrix:

High Impact, Low Effort → DO FIRST (Quick Wins)
High Impact, High Effort → PLAN CAREFULLY (Major Projects)
Low Impact, Low Effort → DO IF TIME (Nice to Have)
Low Impact, High Effort → DON'T DO (Avoid)

docs.title: Common Priorities
docs.text:
Year 1: Foundation - Build staff AI literacy - Implement 2-3 quick wins - Establish governance - Clean data systems

Year 2: Expansion - Scale successful pilots - Integrate tools - Measure ROI - Share learnings

Year 3: Optimization - Advanced applications - Custom solutions - Lead sector innovation - Mentor other organizations

docs.text:

docs.text: Risk Mitigation Staff resistance Early involvement, training, communication Technical failure Pilots, backups, vendor SLAs Budget overruns Phased approach, contingency funds Data breach Security audits, encryption, access controls Vendor lock-in Data portability, open standards Mission drift Regular alignment checks, ethics review

docs.title: Chapter 14: Change Management and Team Training
docs.text:
Leading successful AI adoption.

Learning Objectives: Overcome resistance, train effectively, build AI culture

Time: 3-4 hours

docs.title: Why People Resist AI
docs.text:
Fear: - "AI will replace my job" - "I won't be able to learn this" - "Technology will make mistakes"

Uncertainty: - "What's changing?" - "How will this affect me?" - "Will I have support?"

Loss of Control: - "Someone else is deciding" - "My expertise won't matter" - "I'll lose autonomy"

docs.title: Key Messages
docs.text:
What to emphasize: ✅ AI augments, doesn't replace ✅ Focus on mission impact ✅ Staff input valued ✅ Training provided ✅ Gradual implementation ✅ Celebrate successes

What to avoid: ❌ "AI is smarter than humans" ❌ "This will solve everything" ❌ "You have to adapt" ❌ "It's not negotiable"

docs.title: Chapter 15: AI Governance and the Future
docs.text:
Ensuring responsible, sustainable AI use.

Learning Objectives: Establish governance, prepare for the future, maintain leadership

Time: 4 hours

docs.title: Why Governance Matters
docs.text:
Without governance: - Inconsistent practices - Ethical violations - Security breaches - Mission drift - Wasted resources

With governance: - Clear accountability - Consistent standards - Risk management - Stakeholder trust - Strategic alignment

docs.title: Roles and Responsibilities
docs.text:
AI Steering Committee: - Composition: Executive director, program leads, IT, community members - Responsibilities: Strategy, major decisions, resource allocation - Frequency: Quarterly

AI Ethics Board: - Composition: Diverse stakeholders, external experts - Responsibilities: Ethics review, bias audits, community concerns - Frequency: Bi-annual + as needed

AI Operations Lead: - Role: Day-to-day AI management - Responsibilities: Implementation, training, monitoring - Reports to: Executive team

docs.title: Essential Policies
docs.text:
1. AI Use Policy - When AI is appropriate - Approval processes - Human oversight requirements - Prohibited uses

2. Data Privacy Policy - What data is collected - How it's protected - Who has access - Retention periods

3. Ethics Policy - Core values and principles - Bias testing requirements - Community input process - Complaint procedures

4. Procurement Policy - Vendor evaluation criteria - Security requirements - Contract terms - Exit strategies

docs.title: Emerging Trends (2026-2030)
docs.text:
1. Multimodal AI - Combines text, image, audio, video - More natural interactions - Better accessibility - Richer content

2. Personalization at Scale - True 1:1 communication - Adaptive learning paths - Individualized services - While preserving privacy

3. Autonomous Agents - AI systems that plan and execute - End-to-end task completion - Reduced human intervention - Greater efficiency

4. Smaller, Specialized Models - Custom AI for specific tasks - Lower costs - Faster performance - Better privacy

5. Improved Explainability - Understand AI decisions - Greater transparency - Easier auditing - Increased trust

docs.text:

docs.text:

docs.text: ✅ AI is a tool, not a solution ✅ Mission guides all decisions ✅ Ethics are non-negotiable ✅ Community input is essential ✅ Start small, learn, scale ✅ Technology serves people ✅ The future is collaborative
